questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Under the WHO and IMNCI approach, a child of 2 years with cough and a respiratory rate of 45 per minute with no chest indrawing is classified as:
options: Pneumonia, treated with oral amoxicillin at home
No pneumonia, only a cough or cold
questions.concept: The age-specific cut-offs are 60 per minute under 2 months, 50 from 2 to 12 months and 40 from 1 to 5 years, and fast breathing without indrawing defines pneumonia manageable with oral antibiotics.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Respiratory System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which sign in a child with cough indicates severe pneumonia requiring referral and injectable antibiotics?
options: Lower chest wall indrawing or any general danger sign
questions.concept: Chest indrawing marks increased work of breathing from reduced compliance, and general danger signs are inability to drink, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargy or unconsciousness.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Respiratory System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Bronchiolitis in an infant is most commonly caused by:
questions.concept: Winter epidemics of respiratory syncytial virus cause obstruction of the small airways with hyperinflation, and the illness peaks at 3 to 5 days with recovery over 1 to 2 weeks.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Respiratory System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: The mainstay of treatment for an infant with bronchiolitis is:
options: Supportive care with oxygen, nasal suction and attention to feeding
questions.concept: Trials show no benefit from bronchodilators, steroids or antibiotics in typical bronchiolitis, so management is minimal handling with oxygen and hydration, and nasogastric or intravenous fluids if feeding fails.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Respiratory System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which organism should be suspected in a school-aged child with a persistent dry cough, low-grade fever, patchy infiltrates and a normal-looking child on examination?
questions.concept: The classic mismatch between marked radiographic changes and mild clinical findings gives the name walking pneumonia, and a macrolide is used because the organism has no cell wall.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Respiratory System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 6-month-old with measles develops rapidly worsening pneumonia with pneumatoceles and an empyema on chest radiograph. The likely organism is:
questions.concept: Staphylococcal pneumonia characteristically produces rapid progression with pneumatoceles, empyema and pyopneumothorax, and post-measles immunosuppression is a recognised predisposing factor.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Respiratory System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which measure has the greatest impact on childhood pneumonia mortality at a population level?
options: Pneumococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccination with exclusive breastfeeding
questions.concept: Vaccination against the two commonest bacterial causes, together with breastfeeding, reduced indoor air pollution and zinc for diarrhoea, addresses the determinants rather than the episode.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Respiratory System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 3-year-old presents with sudden onset of coughing and unilateral wheeze with reduced air entry after playing with peanuts. The most appropriate next step is:
options: Rigid bronchoscopy for removal of a foreign body
questions.concept: Unilateral signs of obstruction after a choking episode indicate an inhaled foreign body, most often lodging in the right main bronchus, and a normal radiograph does not exclude it.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Respiratory System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Why is a child with bronchiolitis at higher risk of apnoea than an older child with pneumonia?
options: Immature central respiratory control in infants under 2 months, particularly if preterm
Higher airway resistance from a larger trachea
questions.concept: Apnoea may be the presenting feature in young or preterm infants, which is why age under 2 months and prematurity are indications for admission and monitoring irrespective of oxygen saturation.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Respiratory System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which finding distinguishes empyema requiring drainage from a simple parapneumonic effusion?
options: Frank pus, pH below 7.2, glucose below 40 mg per dL or organisms on Gram stain
A pleural protein above 2 g per dL
questions.concept: These biochemical markers indicate a complicated collection that will loculate and not resolve with antibiotics alone, so intercostal drainage with or without fibrinolytics is required.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Respiratory System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which pattern of findings defines autism spectrum disorder?
options: Persistent deficits in social communication with restricted repetitive behaviours, present from early childhood
questions.concept: The two symptom domains must both be present and must impair function, and early identification matters because intensive behavioural intervention improves outcome.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Behavioural and Developmental Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 7-year-old has inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity present at home and at school for over 6 months, beginning before age 12. The diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Symptoms must be present in more than one setting to exclude situational behaviour, and behavioural parent training with school support is first line in younger children before methylphenidate is considered.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Behavioural and Developmental Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Nocturnal enuresis is defined as involuntary bed-wetting beyond the age of:
questions.concept: Most children achieve night-time continence by 5, and primary monosymptomatic enuresis is managed with reassurance, fluid timing, an enuresis alarm and desmopressin for short-term cover.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Behavioural and Developmental Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 4-year-old with global developmental delay has coarse facies, macroglossia, a large tongue and delayed dentition, with an umbilical hernia. Which screening test is essential?
questions.concept: Congenital hypothyroidism is treatable and its features are easily missed, so a delayed presentation with these signs must prompt thyroid testing; newborn screening detects most cases earlier.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Behavioural and Developmental Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 3-year-old speaks in single words only, does not point to share interest and does not respond to his name, but hearing has not been tested. The essential first investigation is:
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
questions.concept: Hearing impairment is the commonest reversible cause of speech delay and can mimic autism, so audiometry precedes any other investigation in a child with delayed language.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Behavioural and Developmental Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a breath-holding spell from an epileptic seizure in a toddler?
options: A clear precipitant such as pain or anger with cyanosis or pallor preceding the loss of consciousness
questions.concept: Breath-holding spells always have a trigger and the colour change comes first, whereas seizures may occur in sleep with prolonged postictal confusion; iron deficiency is a treatable contributor.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Behavioural and Developmental Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which is the most appropriate first-line management of a 5-year-old with frequent temper tantrums and defiance?
options: Behavioural parent training with consistent limits and positive reinforcement
questions.concept: Structured behavioural approaches are more effective and safer than medication for disruptive behaviour at this age, and medication is reserved for severe aggression after behavioural measures fail.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Behavioural and Developmental Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: An adolescent girl has amenorrhoea, a body mass index of 15 with intense fear of weight gain and excessive exercise. Which complication requires the most urgent monitoring on refeeding?
options: Hypophosphataemia and cardiac failure of the refeeding syndrome
questions.concept: Reintroducing carbohydrate triggers insulin release that drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, so calories are increased gradually with daily electrolyte monitoring and thiamine.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Behavioural and Developmental Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which developmental red flag at 18 months most strongly warrants immediate referral?
options: Loss of previously acquired babbling, gesture or social skills
questions.concept: Regression is never normal at any age and raises the possibility of a neurodegenerative or metabolic disorder as well as autism, so it takes priority over isolated delay in a single milestone.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Behavioural and Developmental Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which principle governs consent for a competent 16-year-old adolescent seeking contraception in India?
options: Confidential counselling should be provided, with the adolescent's best interest and the legal framework on age of consent both considered
Parental consent is always mandatory before any discussion
Contraception can never be provided under 18
questions.concept: Adolescent-friendly services aim to be accessible and confidential while clinicians remain alert to coercion, abuse and mandatory reporting obligations under child protection law.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Behavioural and Developmental Disorders

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which specimen is preferred for microbiological confirmation of pulmonary tuberculosis in a child too young to expectorate?
options: Gastric aspirate or induced sputum for cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification testing
questions.concept: Young children swallow their secretions, so early morning gastric aspirate, induced sputum or a nasopharyngeal aspirate gives the best yield, and molecular testing also reports rifampicin resistance.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Tuberculosis and HIV in Children

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Childhood tuberculosis differs from adult disease in that children more often have:
options: Paucibacillary disease with lymph node and disseminated involvement rather than cavitation
questions.concept: Immaturity of cell-mediated immunity favours haematogenous spread with miliary and meningeal disease, which is why the BCG vaccine targets exactly those severe forms.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Tuberculosis and HIV in Children

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which regimen is recommended for tuberculosis preventive treatment of a 3-year-old household contact of a smear-positive case after active disease is excluded?
options: Isoniazid daily for 6 months, or a shorter rifampicin-containing regimen per current programme guidance
No treatment as the child is asymptomatic
questions.concept: Contacts under 5 are at highest risk of progression to disease, so preventive treatment after excluding active tuberculosis is one of the highest-yield interventions in the programme.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Tuberculosis and HIV in Children

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A child on antitubercular therapy for tuberculous meningitis should also receive:
options: Corticosteroids, which reduce mortality and neurological sequelae
questions.concept: Dexamethasone or prednisolone reduces the inflammatory exudate that causes basal meningeal fibrosis, cranial nerve palsies and hydrocephalus, and this is one of the few clear indications for steroids in tuberculosis.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Tuberculosis and HIV in Children

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which feature on chest radiograph is most characteristic of primary tuberculosis in a child?
options: Hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy, sometimes with airway compression
questions.concept: Nodal enlargement out of proportion to the parenchymal focus is the hallmark, and compression of a bronchus can cause lobar collapse or hyperinflation from a ball-valve effect.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Tuberculosis and HIV in Children

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which finding indicates severe immunosuppression in a child under 5 with HIV, according to WHO staging?
options: A CD4 percentage below 25 percent in a child under 12 months
A CD4 count below 200 cells per microlitre at any age
Weight for age below the third centile
questions.concept: Because absolute CD4 counts are physiologically high and variable in infancy, percentages are used in young children, and infants are treated regardless of counts because progression is rapid.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Tuberculosis and HIV in Children

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which antiretroviral consideration is specific to infants diagnosed with HIV?
options: Antiretroviral therapy is started immediately regardless of clinical or immunological stage
Therapy is deferred until CD4 falls
Therapy is started after 2 years of age
questions.concept: Without treatment about a third of infected infants die in the first year, so early therapy following early infant diagnosis by nucleic acid testing at 6 weeks transformed survival.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Tuberculosis and HIV in Children

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which method is used for early infant diagnosis of HIV in a 6-week-old born to a positive mother?
options: HIV DNA or RNA nucleic acid testing
questions.concept: Maternal IgG persists for up to 18 months so antibody tests cannot distinguish infection from passive transfer, making virological testing essential in the first months of life.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Tuberculosis and HIV in Children

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Why can a tuberculin skin test be negative in a child with miliary tuberculosis?
options: Overwhelming disease suppresses cell-mediated immunity, producing anergy
The antigen is degraded in disseminated disease
The test is only valid after 5 years of age
questions.concept: Other causes of false negatives include HIV, malnutrition, measles, corticosteroids and testing within the window before hypersensitivity develops, so a negative test never excludes tuberculosis.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Tuberculosis and HIV in Children

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which paediatric HIV presentation should prompt testing even without known maternal status?
options: Recurrent severe bacterial infection with failure to thrive, chronic parotid swelling and generalised lymphadenopathy
questions.concept: Persistent generalised lymphadenopathy, parotitis, oral thrush beyond infancy, recurrent severe infection and growth failure are the classic clinical clues to vertically acquired HIV.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Tuberculosis and HIV in Children

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Congenital & rheumatic heart disease in children
questions.stem: Which is the commonest congenital heart defect in children?
questions.concept: Ventricular septal defect accounts for around a third of congenital heart disease, and small muscular defects often close spontaneously in the first years of life.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Cardiovascular System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Congenital & rheumatic heart disease in children
questions.stem: Which congenital heart lesion is the commonest cause of cyanotic heart disease presenting after infancy?
questions.concept: Transposition presents in the first days of life, whereas the degree of pulmonary stenosis in tetralogy determines the age of presentation, and squatting increases systemic resistance to reduce the right-to-left shunt.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Cardiovascular System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Congenital & rheumatic heart disease in children
questions.stem: A neonate is deeply cyanosed on day 1 with a single loud second sound and an egg-on-side cardiac silhouette. The immediate life-saving measure is:
options: Prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency, with consideration of balloon atrial septostomy
Immediate corrective surgery in the first hour
questions.concept: In transposition survival depends on mixing, so keeping the duct open and enlarging the atrial communication buys time until an arterial switch operation.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Cardiovascular System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Congenital & rheumatic heart disease in children
questions.stem: Which lesion produces a continuous machinery murmur with bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure in a preterm infant?
questions.concept: Failure of ductal closure is common in prematurity and causes a left-to-right shunt with pulmonary overcirculation, and indomethacin, ibuprofen or paracetamol is used to close it.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Cardiovascular System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Congenital & rheumatic heart disease in children
questions.stem: A 6-year-old has a continuous murmur, differential blood pressure between arms and legs, and rib notching on radiograph. The diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Collateral intercostal vessels erode the ribs over years, and the association with Turner syndrome and with bicuspid aortic valve means both should be sought.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Cardiovascular System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Congenital & rheumatic heart disease in children
questions.stem: Which finding distinguishes an innocent murmur from a pathological one in a child?
options: A soft systolic murmur that varies with posture, with normal pulses, no thrill and a normal second sound
A grade 4 murmur with a thrill
A continuous murmur with a fixed split second sound
questions.concept: Innocent murmurs are systolic, soft, position-dependent and unaccompanied by other signs, whereas any diastolic murmur, thrill or abnormal second sound requires echocardiography.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Cardiovascular System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Congenital & rheumatic heart disease in children
questions.stem: According to the revised Jones criteria, which change was made for populations at high risk of rheumatic fever such as India?
options: Subclinical carditis on echocardiography counts as a major criterion and monoarthritis or polyarthralgia may substitute for polyarthritis
Chorea was removed as a major criterion
Two minor criteria alone became sufficient
questions.concept: Recognising echocardiographic carditis and lower joint thresholds improves sensitivity where the disease burden is high, at some cost in specificity.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Cardiovascular System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Congenital & rheumatic heart disease in children
questions.stem: Secondary prophylaxis after an attack of rheumatic fever without carditis should continue for:
options: 5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer
questions.concept: Duration is graded by the presence and severity of carditis, extending to 10 years or age 21 with carditis and often lifelong with residual valve disease.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Cardiovascular System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Congenital & rheumatic heart disease in children
questions.stem: Which congenital lesion is associated with maternal lithium use, and what is the classic echocardiographic finding?
options: Ebstein anomaly, with apical displacement of the tricuspid valve and a large right atrium
Tetralogy of Fallot with a boot-shaped heart
questions.concept: Downward displacement of the septal and posterior tricuspid leaflets atrialises the right ventricle, causing tricuspid regurgitation and often an associated atrial communication with right-to-left shunting.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Cardiovascular System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Congenital & rheumatic heart disease in children
questions.stem: Why does a large ventricular septal defect present at 6 to 8 weeks rather than at birth?
options: Pulmonary vascular resistance falls over the first weeks, so the left-to-right shunt and its symptoms increase
The ductus closes at that time
questions.concept: At birth right and left pressures are nearly equal so shunting is minimal, and heart failure appears as resistance falls; this is why the murmur may also become louder with time.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Cardiovascular System

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Fluid & electrolyte therapy and diarrhoeal disease in children
questions.stem: Which osmolarity characterises the WHO-recommended reduced osmolarity oral rehydration solution?
options: About 245 mOsm per litre with 75 mmol sodium and 75 mmol glucose
questions.concept: The lower osmolarity reduces stool output, vomiting and the need for unscheduled intravenous fluid compared with the older formulation, without increasing hyponatraemia.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Diarrhoeal Diseases and Fluid Therapy

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Fluid & electrolyte therapy and diarrhoeal disease in children
questions.stem: A 9-month-old is treated for acute diarrhoea. For how long, and at what dose, should zinc be continued after the diarrhoea stops?
options: 14 days in total at 20 mg daily
questions.concept: The full 14-day course is what reduces recurrence over the following two to three months, and infants under 6 months receive 10 mg daily; stopping when stools settle loses most of the benefit.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Diarrhoeal Diseases and Fluid Therapy

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Fluid & electrolyte therapy and diarrhoeal disease in children
questions.stem: A child with diarrhoea is restless and irritable with sunken eyes, drinks eagerly and has a skin pinch that goes back slowly. The classification and plan are:
options: Some dehydration, treated with oral rehydration solution under supervision (Plan B)
questions.concept: Two or more of these signs define some dehydration, requiring about 75 mL per kg of oral rehydration solution over 4 hours with reassessment, whereas lethargy or inability to drink indicates severe dehydration.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Diarrhoeal Diseases and Fluid Therapy

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Fluid & electrolyte therapy and diarrhoeal disease in children
questions.stem: In severe dehydration in a child over 12 months, the recommended intravenous regimen is:
options: Ringer lactate 100 mL per kg, giving 30 mL per kg in the first 30 minutes then 70 mL per kg over 2.5 hours
Normal saline 20 mL per kg once only
Dextrose 5 percent 100 mL per kg over 6 hours
questions.concept: Infants under 12 months receive the same total volume but more slowly, with the first 30 mL per kg over 1 hour, and reassessment guides repetition of the bolus.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Diarrhoeal Diseases and Fluid Therapy

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Fluid & electrolyte therapy and diarrhoeal disease in children
questions.stem: A 2-year-old with acute watery diarrhoea is brought by parents requesting a stool test and an antibiotic. He is alert with no dehydration. The correct advice is:
options: No stool test or antibiotic is needed; give oral rehydration solution, zinc and continued feeding
Send a stool culture and start ciprofloxacin
Give an antimotility agent to reduce stool frequency
Withhold feeds for 24 hours to rest the bowel
questions.concept: Most acute watery diarrhoea is viral and self-limiting, routine stool culture changes nothing, antimotility drugs are contraindicated in children, and withholding feeds worsens nutrition and mucosal recovery.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Diarrhoeal Diseases and Fluid Therapy

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Fluid & electrolyte therapy and diarrhoeal disease in children
questions.stem: Which electrolyte abnormality should be anticipated in a malnourished child with prolonged diarrhoea and is a common cause of persistent lethargy?
questions.concept: Total body potassium is depleted by stool losses and by malnutrition itself, so oral rehydration solution and potassium supplementation are given, and correction is essential before nutritional rehabilitation.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Diarrhoeal Diseases and Fluid Therapy

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Fluid & electrolyte therapy and diarrhoeal disease in children
questions.stem: Which fluid is preferred in a child with severe acute malnutrition who is in shock, and why?
options: Half-strength Darrow solution with dextrose or Ringer lactate with dextrose, given cautiously because of the risk of cardiac failure
Full-volume rapid Ringer lactate bolus as in a normally nourished child
Normal saline 40 mL per kg rapidly
questions.concept: Myocardial function and sodium handling are impaired in severe malnutrition, so slower, smaller boluses with close monitoring for pulmonary oedema are used, and ReSoMal is preferred for oral rehydration.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Diarrhoeal Diseases and Fluid Therapy

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Fluid & electrolyte therapy and diarrhoeal disease in children
questions.stem: Persistent diarrhoea in a child is defined as an episode lasting:
questions.concept: Persistent diarrhoea carries a high mortality because of coexisting malnutrition, and management centres on a lactose-reduced diet, micronutrients and treating specific infections rather than on antimotility drugs.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Diarrhoeal Diseases and Fluid Therapy

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Fluid & electrolyte therapy and diarrhoeal disease in children
questions.stem: Why does glucose in oral rehydration solution enhance sodium and water absorption even when the enterocyte is damaged by cholera toxin?
options: The sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT1 remains intact and drives coupled sodium absorption with osmotic water movement
questions.concept: Cholera toxin increases chloride secretion but does not damage the absorptive cotransporter, which is the physiological insight that made oral rehydration therapy possible and saved millions of lives.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Diarrhoeal Diseases and Fluid Therapy

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.topic: Fluid & electrolyte therapy and diarrhoeal disease in children
questions.stem: A child with diarrhoea develops seizures and a serum sodium of 160 mmol per litre. Correction must be gradual because:
options: Rapid lowering of sodium causes cerebral oedema as water shifts into brain cells that have accumulated osmolytes
questions.concept: In hypernatraemia the brain accumulates idiogenic osmoles, so sodium is lowered by no more than 10 to 12 mmol per litre per day; osmotic demyelination is the hazard of correcting chronic hyponatraemia too fast.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Ch. Diarrhoeal Diseases and Fluid Therapy
